profile.address: 65, Kreiger Lane, J. B. Williams Co. Historic District, Glastonbury Center, Glastonbury, Capitol Planning Region, Connecticut, 06033
profile.reading:
This entry corresponds to 65 Kreiger Lane in Glastonbury, Connecticut, a small industrial/flex building in a light-industrial pocket off the Route 2 corridor near several similarly sized multi-tenant flex buildings, most built in the late 1980s of masonry construction, that local commercial brokers refer to collectively as the Kreiger Lane industrial area. Real-estate trade coverage of a September 2014 sale records that EGI Properties, LLC, an entity tied to the listed operator, Ergonomic Group, Inc. (also known as EGI), purchased the roughly 9,800-square-foot building at this address for $980,000, explicitly to house the company's Connecticut operations. That transaction is the strongest publicly available link between this specific address and the operator named in this registry record.

Ergonomic Group is an IT technology-solutions and managed-support provider serving financial-services, healthcare, government, and utility clients, headquartered at 200 Robbins Lane in Jericho, New York. The company's own site emphasizes its New York base and does not describe a Connecticut facility, let alone a data center, among its locations. That omission is not unusual for a firm of this kind: managed-services companies often maintain a secondary regional office, for staff, a local network-operations presence, or client-facing support, without publicizing it as a distinct facility, particularly one this small and this far from headquarters.

Given the building's modest size (under 10,000 square feet, per the 2014 sale record) and its classification as flex/light-industrial rather than raised-floor technical space, it reads far more plausibly as a regional branch office or a support and staging location for Ergonomic Group's Connecticut-area client engagements than as a colocation or hyperscale data center in the industry sense of the term. The surrounding stretch of Glastonbury, historically tied to 19th-century industrial development along this part of town, is now a mixed light-industrial and residential area rather than a data-center corridor.

No power capacity, cooling system, tenant list, or server-room square footage for this address has been published by Ergonomic Group, by the town, or by any trade or local-news source identified in this research. That absence is itself informative: it is consistent with a small, company-owned regional operations office rather than a marketed or purpose-built data center facility, and nothing found here should be read as confirming that mission-critical IT infrastructure at data-center scale is housed at this address.

This confirms a genuine, sourced tie between this address and the named operator; it is not a data-center-scale building (under 10,000 sq ft, flex/light-industrial), and no operator, county, or press source describes any data-center-specific infrastructure at this address. research_status remains complete.

reading.body:
This address is a roughly 9,800-square-foot flex and light-industrial building in Glastonbury, Connecticut, purchased by an entity tied to Ergonomic Group in 2014 for regional office operations, not a data center. No power capacity, cooling infrastructure, or server space has been published by the operator, the municipality, or any trade source. The building's modest size and construction type are consistent with a managed-services company's regional branch or client-support staging location rather than a purpose-built or colocation facility.

Connecticut has five mapped data center facilities statewide, of which only two have published power specifications totaling 8 megawatts. This Glastonbury address, ranked third by claimed published capacity in the state, has disclosed no megawatt figure of its own. The absence of any published specification for this site, combined with its industrial-office classification, suggests it does not belong in a data-center registry at all.

This facility does not represent meaningful data center capacity for AI infrastructure. A small regional office cannot serve the grid-scale power draw, redundant cooling, or density of compute that the thesis of this site requires to matter in AI scaling. Its inclusion in state-level counts would misrepresent the actual technical capacity available in Connecticut for mission-critical workloads.
